limitations: required_capabilities lists coarse prerequisites for checking each obligation, including unmapped obligations, rather than exhaustive target implementation dependencies. Tags follow the cited public contracts and the stated observations. Fixture repository operations require local-repository; merely querying configuration does not require app execution. A runnable-content preservation assertion does require sandbox-execution even when its primary command is info or uninstall. installation permits any installation profile, while user-installation and system-installation select specific profiles. system-authorization covers authorized system changes or explicit privilege checks, not ordinary read-only system queries. Session services, fault injection and other specialized capabilities are included only where the obligation needs them; alternative fixture provisioning may have additional prerequisites.

This is a curated, source-backed behavior obligation catalogue, not all CLI behavior. Every active canonical command has at least one obligation, but neither command presence nor option presence means its behavior is fully covered. The complete mechanical command/option denominator is separate.

Granularity varies with the observable contract. Rows are not weighted by complexity, risk, or frequency, and a percentage over these rows measures only this catalogue. No test credits or execution results are assigned here.

Sources are repository public manpage documents. Anchors identify section titles, option text, or quoted prose after XML text normalization. app/flatpak-main.c was consulted only to identify active canonical command names; hidden deprecated aliases and the separate flatpak-spawn executable are outside this scope.

The command descriptions support lifecycle operations, but do not expressly specify the full error/recovery contracts retained at the user's request: cli.install.user.missing-ref, cli.info.user.absent-ref, cli.uninstall.user.absent-ref, cli.update.user.failed-download-preserves, cli.update.user.noop, and cli.update.user.retry. Their nonzero statuses, diagnostic identification, unchanged deployments, and successful retry/no-op expectations are compatibility obligations inferred from those operations, not verbatim documented guarantees. The docs do not prescribe the runner's accepted diagnostic strings or its payload request pattern.

cli.install.user.already-installed is grounded in the documented warning-and-ignore behavior under --or-update; an explicit zero exit status is not stated there. cli.install.user.runtime-dependency is supported by the dependency options and runtime-resolution documentation, rather than a detailed dependency transaction specification. Empty enumeration and unsuccessful absent-ref queries are consequences of the documented query domains, not specified output byte layouts.

User and system are selected installation profiles, not privilege levels. Session document/permission and running-instance commands are any because they do not select an installation; they still operate in a user's session. Build/repository commands are any when their result is independent of the installation providing prerequisites. Explicit system obligations require separate evidence and remain untested by the existing user-only scenarios.

Known omissions include exhaustive partial-ref/fuzzy-match and interactive choice cases, option ordering and repeated-option precedence, every output column and ellipsization mode, localization and terminal formatting, cancellation/crash/concurrency and disk-full recovery, and combinations across architectures, branches, remotes and installations.

Sandbox obligations sample filesystem, environment, network, bus and conditional permissions. They do not enumerate every socket, device, feature, USB query, namespace, nested sandbox, permission-layer interaction or parental-control policy. Document/permission obligations do not enumerate every portal-specific table schema or desktop integration.

Distribution obligations do not enumerate OCI transports/compression, authenticators, redirects, mirror selection, every signature failure mode, extra-data scripts, extension/subset rules, all static-delta strategies, or every vendor preinstall/configuration key. Build options are represented by selected output contracts, not one generated row per flag.

Manpage inconsistencies are not resolved through private code: run's --nousb term differs from its prose and build-finish's query syntax; the global Commands section omits active commands such as preinstall, which has its own manpage. Omitted disputed details should not be inferred as tested contracts. Version-specific features require evidence from a target that supports them.

requirements.description: Installing an available application ref in the user installation succeeds and makes application version A installed and queryable.
Installing a user application with an available, initially absent required runtime also installs the declared runtime ref and its expected commit.
Querying an installed user ref with --show-ref and --show-commit returns the exact requested full ref and its installed commit in machine-readable output.
Running an installed user application executes the command declared in its metadata and delivers that command's expected output.
Updating a user application when version B is the branch tip succeeds, makes B the installed commit, and runs B's contents.

sources.anchor: Normally, this command updates the application to the tip of its branch.

requirements.description: An update whose required application payload cannot be downloaded fails and leaves the previously installed application A and its runtime at their prior commits, with A still runnable.
Updating a user application already at the branch tip succeeds without changing its installed app/runtime commits or runnable contents.

sources.anchor: Normally, this command updates the application to the tip of its branch.

requirements.description: Installing an already installed user application without --or-update succeeds with an already-installed warning and keeps A installed and runnable even when B is available.
Installing a nonexistent full ref fails with a diagnostic identifying the requested application as unavailable and leaves a fresh user installation's ref enumeration empty.

Querying a ref absent from the user installation fails with a diagnostic identifying that ref as not installed, while an unrelated installed app and runtime retain their commits and runnable contents.

sources.anchor: Show info about an installed application or runtime.

requirements.description: Uninstalling a ref absent from the user installation fails with a diagnostic identifying that ref as not installed, while an unrelated installed app and runtime retain their commits and runnable contents.
Uninstalling an installed user application succeeds and makes that application unavailable to an installed-ref query.
Application-only enumeration succeeds with no application entries when no user applications remain, even if a runtime is still installed.
Enumeration of the empty user installation succeeds with no installed application or runtime entries.

sources.anchor: Lists the names of the installed applications and runtimes.

requirements.description: After a required payload download failure, retrying the user update once the source is available succeeds in fetching the needed data and installs runnable version B with the expected app/runtime commits.
Installing an already installed user ref with --or-update updates it to the available branch tip.
Installing a valid .flatpak single-file bundle deploys the application carried by that bundle in the user installation.
Installing from a valid .flatpakref application description installs the application identified by that description.
Installing with --no-deploy downloads the latest ref contents without making the ref installed as a deployment.
Installing with --no-pull deploys locally available ref contents without downloading a newer remote version.
Updating with --commit deploys the specified available commit rather than the branch tip, including when selecting an older version.
A user update with no ref updates all eligible installed apps and runtimes to their available branch tips.

sources.anchor: If no REF is given, everything is updated

requirements.description: An update whose partial ref matches multiple installed user refs fails with an error listing the alternatives.

sources.anchor: if there are multiple matches an error message will list the alternatives.

requirements.description: Uninstalling an app with --delete-data removes its data under ~/.var/app and its permissions in the permission store.
Uninstalling with --unused removes an unpinned runtime that is no longer needed by any installed application.
Installing with no installation selector deploys the requested application in the default system-wide installation.

sources.anchor: Unless overridden with the --user or the --installation option

requirements.description: Installing with --installation=NAME deploys the requested ref in the named configured system installation rather than the default installation.
Updating with --system updates the matching ref in the default system installation while leaving a separately installed user copy unchanged.
Uninstalling with --system removes the matching system deployment while retaining a separately installed user copy.
Uninstalling without an installation selector fails when the requested ref is installed in both the default system and user installations.

sources.anchor: errors out if it exists in more than one.

requirements.description: Adding a named user remote with a repository URL persists that name and URL so a later remotes query reports the same pair.
The title supplied when adding a user remote persists and is returned unchanged by a later remotes title query.
The numeric priority supplied when adding a user remote persists and is reported by a later remotes priority query.
Adding an existing user remote from a repository URL with --if-not-exists leaves its previously configured URL, title and priority unchanged despite different supplied values.
Adding a remote from a .flatpakrepo description configures the repository URL and title defined by that description.
Adding an existing remote from a .flatpakrepo file with --if-not-exists replaces its filter with the file's Filter value, or clears the existing filter when the file omits Filter.
Listing user remotes returns configured remotes in priority order, with higher numeric priorities first.

sources.anchor: Lists the known remote repositories, in priority order.

requirements.description: A remotes query selecting name,url,title,priority returns the configured values for those fields in the requested column order.
A user remotes query with --show-disabled includes a configured disabled remote.
Changing a user remote's URL persists the new URL, which a subsequent remotes URL query reports for that remote.
Changing a user remote's title persists the replacement title, which a subsequent remotes title query reports.
Changing a user remote's priority persists the replacement number, which a subsequent remotes priority query reports.
Disabling a user remote persists its disabled state, preventing automatic updates from that remote in a later update invocation.
Enabling a disabled user remote persists its enabled state so a later update can obtain an available update from it.
A configured user remote filter denies refs matching a deny rule except refs explicitly matched by an allow rule.
Deleting an unused user remote persists its removal: later remotes enumeration, including disabled remotes, contains no entry for that name while other remotes remain configured.
Deleting a user remote with --force removes its configuration even when installed apps or runtimes use it.
Adding a remote with --system persists it in the default system configuration and does not create a user remote of that name.
A remotes query with --installation=NAME lists the remotes configured in the named system installation.
remote-ls reports the available application and runtime refs from the specified configured user remote, including refs not installed locally.
remote-ls --updates reports only refs with updates available, excluding installed refs already at their remote tip.
A remote-info machine-readable query returns the matched full ref and its remote commit ID, rather than the commit of an older local deployment.
remote-info --log displays available previous versions of the requested remote ref.
Searching user remotes for matching text returns the applications or runtimes described by their AppStream data.
Updating AppStream for a specified user remote makes its updated application descriptions available to subsequent search.
info --show-metadata returns the metadata belonging to the installed user application or runtime.
info --file-access reports the application's level of access to the requested path in machine-readable output.
Listing with --app-runtime returns installed user applications using the specified runtime and excludes applications using another runtime.
Listing with --system reports default system-installed refs and excludes refs installed only in the user installation.
Setting the user languages configuration persists the supplied value, which a later config --get languages returns.
Unsetting languages removes the explicit user setting so locale inclusion again follows extra-languages and the current locale.
A configuration change with --installation=NAME is stored in that named system installation rather than another installation.
An installed user ref matching a stored mask pattern remains at its current version when an update is available.

sources.anchor: A masked ref will never be updated or automatically installed

requirements.description: Removing a stored user mask pattern removes it from later mask enumeration.

sources.anchor: To list the current set of masks

requirements.description: A user runtime matching a stored pin remains installed when unused runtimes are automatically removed.

sources.anchor: A pinned ref will never be automatically uninstalled

requirements.description: Removing a user pin pattern removes it from later pin enumeration.

sources.anchor: To list the current set of pins

requirements.description: When the relevant journal records are available, user history reports the installation, update and removal changes made to user refs.
Repairing a user installation reinstalls deployed refs whose required repository objects are missing or invalid, restoring usable deployed content when the source is available.
Repair --dry-run reports installation inconsistencies without changing the installation.
Repair of the system installation requires root privileges; an unprivileged invocation cannot perform the system repair.

sources.anchor: flatpak repair has to be run with root privileges to operate on the system installation.

requirements.description: Preinstall with no action options synchronizes system-installed vendor flatpaks with the selected .preinstall definitions by installing or removing the designated refs.
A vendor-preinstalled flatpak explicitly uninstalled by the user is not automatically reinstalled by a later preinstall synchronization.

sources.anchor: Users can opt out of preinstalled flatpaks by simply uninstalling them

requirements.description: Arguments after the application ref are passed to the application command in the sandbox.

sources.anchor: Extra arguments are passed on to the application.

requirements.description: run --command executes the specified sandbox command instead of the command declared in application metadata.
The launched user application sees its application files at /app and its declared runtime files at /usr.
Application writes to its writable /var storage remain available on a later run of the same app.

sources.anchor: a writable directory at /var, whose content is preserved between application runs.

requirements.description: An environment variable explicitly set with run --env has the supplied value inside the application, overriding its metadata value.
With --clear-env, an ordinary inherited host variable is absent from the sandbox while explicitly set application variables still apply.
A host path granted solely with --filesystem=PATH:ro is readable inside the app but cannot be written there.
run --nofilesystem=host:reset removes filesystem grants inherited from metadata and stored overrides, so a path available only through those grants is inaccessible.
run --unshare=network prevents sharing the host network subsystem despite a network share granted in application metadata.
Granting --talk-name for a session-bus service permits the sandboxed application to talk to that service through the filtered session bus.
A socket granted only through --socket-if is exposed when its runtime condition is true and is not exposed by that grant when the condition is false.
With --file-forwarding, file arguments between @@ markers are replaced by document-portal paths that give the application nonpersistent read/write access.
run --system executes the default system-installed application even when a different version of the same ref is installed for the user.
A per-app user environment override persists across invocations and changes that variable in subsequent application runs.
override --show APP reports the stored overrides for the specified application.
override --reset APP removes that app's stored overrides so they no longer affect subsequent launches.
Making an installed user app branch current makes that branch's exported files visible to the host and selects it for runs without an explicit branch.

sources.anchor: The current branch and arch of the application is used

requirements.description: ps reports a running Flatpak instance with its instance ID, application ID and corresponding process IDs in the selected columns.
Entering an identified running sandbox creates a command process in that sandbox with the same environment and forwards its extra arguments.
Killing a running Flatpak by its instance ID stops that instance.
Exporting a local file for an app creates a document ID and lets that app read the file through the document portal despite lacking direct host-path access.
Exporting a previously exported file with --unique creates a different document ID instead of reusing its existing ID.
Revoking an app's document write permission with --forbid-write prevents that app from writing through its document grant.
documents lists exported files with their document IDs and full origin paths.
documents APPID lists only files exported to that application, excluding documents granted only to another app.
document-info reports an exported file's document ID, FUSE path, original location and per-application permissions consistently with its current grant.
Unexporting a file removes its document ID and makes that document unavailable to all sandboxed applications.
Unexporting with --doc-id removes the specified document even when its original file has been deleted.
Setting an application's permissions for a table/object entry stores the supplied permission strings so a later permission query returns them.
permission-set --data associates the supplied serialized GVariant with the specified permission-store entry.
permissions TABLE ID returns the requested entry from that table rather than entries for other object IDs or tables.
permission-show lists the dynamic permissions stored for the requested application.
Removing permissions with an APP_ID removes only that application's entry for the selected table/object, retaining another application's entry.
Removing a permission-store table/object entry without APP_ID removes the entire selected object entry.
Resetting permissions for an application removes all of its permissions across the permission store.
build-init creates a build directory with metadata identifying the requested app, SDK and runtime, and empty files and var subdirectories.
build-init without --update reports an error for a directory already initialized as a build directory.

sources.anchor: It is an error to run build-init on a directory that has already been initialized

requirements.description: A build command uses the declared SDK at /usr and can write artifacts through /app and /var that persist in the build directory across commands.
build --readonly prevents the command from changing the normally writable build destination directories.
Finalizing an initialized build copies eligible desktop files, icons, D-Bus service files and AppStream metainfo from files into the export subdirectory.
build-finish --command records the supplied default launch command in the metadata Application group.
build-finish reports an error when the directory has not been initialized or has already been finalized.

sources.anchor: It is an error to run build-finish

requirements.description: Exporting a finalized app creates the app/APPNAME/ARCH/BRANCH repository commit containing files, export and metadata while excluding other build-directory contents.
build-export --runtime exports a runtime using the build directory's usr subtree as its files.
build-bundle creates the requested single-file bundle carrying the selected application branch from the local repository, suitable for bundle installation or import.
A bundle created with --repo-url configures a remote for that URL when installed, providing the application's update source.
Importing a valid build-bundle output makes its ref and contents available in the destination repository.
build-sign adds a signature from the requested GPG key to the selected local application or runtime commit, verifiable with that key's public material.
Updating repository metadata generates a summary that makes the repository's current refs discoverable through remote-ls.
build-update-repo --prune removes unreferenced repository objects.
build-commit-from creates a destination-branch commit with the selected source branch's contents without importing the source's parent history or signatures.
repo --branches lists the branches present in the specified local repository.
repo --metadata prints the metadata for the selected branch of the local repository.
create-usb copies selected user refs with dependencies and metadata so a destination with the matching collection-ID remotes configured can install those refs offline from the copied repository.
The global --help option prints help options and exits.
The global --version option prints version information and exits.
The global --default-arch option prints the host's default Flatpak architecture and exits.
The global --supported-arches option prints supported architectures in priority order and exits.
The global --gl-drivers option prints the active GL driver list and exits.
Verbose command processing emits debug information, with repeated verbosity providing additional detail for operations that have it.
The global --ostree-verbose option emits OSTree debug information during commands that perform OSTree operations.
The global --installations option prints paths of configured system installations and exits.
The global --print-updated-env option prints the environment variables needed to use Flatpaks, amending the current environment.
Combining --print-system-only with --print-updated-env produces environment settings for system installations without including the user's home installation.
